appendix/J_future.tex: \subsection{Smaller convolutional networks} The strongest global-efficiency models use the fine EM2 input, but their parameter counts exceed those of the compact MLPs. The first step is therefore compression rather than greater depth: reduce channel counts and dense-head widths, then test pruning, quantisation-aware training and knowledge distillation into a student of roughly $2{,}000$ parameters. The dense head contains most parameters and is a natural pruning target. Structured reductions should be evaluated alongside sparse pruning, because fewer nonzero weights do not automatically imply lower hardware cost.

Each candidate should retain the event-level calibration protocol and report the full energy-efficiency profile, not just global efficiency. An FPGA-oriented toolchain such as hls4ml can then assess synthesis feasibility, supported operations, latency and resource use. Quantisation and compression may change score ordering, so calibration and efficiency must be re-evaluated after conversion. The present parameter counts are not hardware measurements, and small accuracy losses cannot be assumed in advance (\cref{app:hardware_scope}).

\subsection{Adaptive, representation-aware objectives} The constrained objective used manually specified regions, floors and update rates. A continuation is to derive rewarded regions and allowed deficits from the measured weaknesses of the pretrained model, and scale multiplier updates according to each region's statistical resolution. Region choices must remain tied to physics priorities: automatically optimising only the easiest deficiencies would reproduce the trade-offs the constraints were intended to prevent.

Loss and representation should also be studied jointly. IF helped several compact-input configurations, whereas plain BCE followed by fine-tuning gave the highest global efficiency on the richest tested inputs. A modular objective could adapt to the starting score distribution and representation while preserving the requirements in \cref{app:loss_requirements}. Any data-driven choices must use training or validation data, with a held-out evaluation after the choices are fixed.

\subsection{Whole-event architectures and object multiplicity} A whole-event model could learn which candidates belong together and whether their joint geometry is consistent with a tau event. Study architectures that process a variable-size set of candidate features and scores, using permutation-invariant aggregation or an explicitly relational mechanism. Vary the number of retained objects to measure the value of context against latency and resource cost; use masking for absent candidates rather than treating padding as physical input.

Pairwise angular separations, relative energies and correlations among shower shapes can then affect a joint event decision instead of being attached to independent object scores. Define whether the output is an event score or context-aware object scores, and match both approaches at the same event-level background rate. Preserve event-level splits and report the event metric as well as compatible object-level efficiencies. The current sample retains at most six TOBs: testing candidates beyond that limit requires a new extraction, not merely changing the model's input size. This direction extends the single-object study and should be coordinated with the team's pair-object work.

\subsection{Richer inputs for the low-energy region} Low-energy taus remained difficult across substantially different models, and shared errors suggest that the current representation is a limiting factor, though they do not establish a fundamental information bound (\cref{app:analysis_capacity}). Candidate additions include finer granularity in non-EM2 layers, wider calorimeter windows, timing or tracking quantities and neighbouring-object context. These are options to investigate only where detector readout and the intended trigger stage make them available.

The existing $12\times12$ EM2 image resolves the same angular region as the coarse core tensor; it is not already a wider-window measurement. Separate added spatial coverage from added granularity in controlled comparisons, and assess gains within low-energy bins at the fixed event rate. Any new input must justify its acquisition, preprocessing and hardware cost as well as its predictive benefit.

sections/04_methodology.tex: \section{Methodology} \label{sec:method} To support the changing hardware requirements of \cref{sec:setting}, we studied four complementary axes: data and features (\cref{sec:features}), classifier and loss (\cref{sec:loss}), architecture (\cref{sec:arch}) and the input unit (\cref{sec:input_unit}). Matched comparisons isolate individual mechanisms where possible. Models are named by their inputs, architecture and training objective; \cref{tab:naming} (\cref{app:naming}) explains every name.

\subsection{Data exploration and feature engineering} \label{sec:features} We compared class-normalised distributions of $\tau$ and non-$\tau$ objects on the training split, overall and within the $\ptTOB$ intervals $[5,10)$, $[10,20)$, $[20,40)$, $[40,80)$ and $[80,120)\GeV$. A variable carries information beyond energy only if the classes still differ \emph{inside} each interval. All features live in a modular registry and are selected by configuration (\cref{app:features}).

\paragraph{Energy: a strong separator and a shortcut.} $\ptTOB$ is the strongest single separator (\cref{fig:features}a). Non-$\tau$ objects pile up at the $\SI{5}{GeV}$ threshold, while $\tau$ objects have a long tail. For the same reason it is a \emph{shortcut}: a network trained with BCE lowers its loss by learning the energy scale and has little incentive to learn the weaker, complementary shape information. This observation motivated the classifier of \cref{sec:loss}.

\paragraph{EM2 compactness.} The most useful engineered variable is the fraction of the $12\times12$ EM2 energy contained in its most energetic $3\times3$ cell window: \begin{equation} \Frac=\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}\sum_{(a,b)\in w}E_{ab}\Big/\sum_{a,b}E_{ab}, \label{eq:frac} \end{equation} where $\mathcal{W}$ is the set of the $100$ overlapping $3\times3$ windows (\cref{fig:features}c,d). A cell window is smaller than one tower, so $\Frac$ measures compactness at a granularity the core tensor cannot resolve. Unlike $\ptTOB$, its separation persists within fixed energy intervals and grows with energy (\cref{fig:features}b, \cref{fig:frac_conditioned}).

\begin{figure}[t] \centering \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_features.pdf} \caption{Feature study (training split, normalised per class). (a) $\ptTOB$, log scale. (b) $\Frac$ for $20\leq\ptTOB<\SI{40}{GeV}$; dashed lines mark the medians. (c,d) Computation of $\Frac$ for the objects of \cref{fig:calo_input}: the red square is the best $3\times3$ window.} \label{fig:features} \end{figure}

\paragraph{Inputs used below.} Besides $\Frac$ (\Ffeat), four inputs stayed competitive at the operating point: the 45 raw core cells (\CT), the strongest single input throughout; 15 per-layer summaries (\SUM), which are the sum $S_\ell$, the dominance $2M_\ell-S_\ell$ ($M_\ell$ the maximum cell) and the sparsity $\#\{\text{cells}>0.1M_\ell\}$ of each layer~\cite{kernan2026}; the ``core physics'' vector (\CP): BDT score, $\ptTOB$, and $\eta,\phi$ relative to the leading TOB; and the EM2 image, which only the CNNs read. Event-topology variables (the $\ptTOB$ sum, the second-highest $\ptTOB$, the separation of the two leading TOBs) clearly separate events by $\tau$ multiplicity. However, they take the same value for every object of an event, cannot rank the objects within it, and did not improve on object-level inputs at $\FPRtarget$ (\cref{sec:input_unit}, \cref{app:features}).

\subsection{Classifier and loss design} \label{sec:loss} BCE measures the average quality of object-level probabilities. The trigger instead depends on the far tail of the \emph{event-level} background distribution and has explicit requirements per energy region. We addressed this mismatch in three steps, each changing one mechanism: the decision rule, the signal weighting and the training objective.

\paragraph{The TOB--NN OR classifier.} Instead of asking a network to relearn the energy threshold, we pair it with the deterministic TOB comparator: accept an object through either branch, then require two accepted objects per event, \begin{equation} a_{e,i}=\1[\ptTOBof{e,i}\geq C]\vee\1[s_{e,i}\geq t],\qquad A_e=\1\Big[\textstyle\sum_i a_{e,i}\geq2\Big]. \label{eq:or} \end{equation} The TOB branch protects the high-energy plateau; the NN supplies complementary shape-based decisions. Thresholds are calibrated jointly, counting mixed-branch events exactly. Validation selects the TOB budget $b$ to maximise the equally weighted efficiency gain across $25$--$100\GeV$, subject to the event fake-rate limit and regional protection guards. A smaller selected $b^\star$ suggests less reliance on the comparator, not a standalone measure of NN quality. Training remains (weighted) BCE; the OR changes the decision rule only. \Cref{app:or} gives the objective, cross-fitted calibration, guards and earlier two-expert trial.

\paragraph{Spectrum-aware signal weighting.} We reweight each object's contribution to binary cross-entropy: \begin{equation} \mathcal L_{\mathrm{wBCE}}=-\frac1N\sum_i w_i\big[y_i\log s_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-s_i)\big], \label{eq:weighted_bce} \end{equation} where $y_i$ is the signal label and $s_i$ the NN score. Background keeps $w_i=1$; for signal, $w_i=r(t_i)/\langle r\rangle_{\mathrm{train},S}$, with truth momentum $t_i$ in GeV. Mean-one normalisation preserves the total signal weight while redistributing its gradient across energies. We compare two raw profiles: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} r_{\mathrm{IF}}(t)&=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\bar n/n_{k(t)},\,0.2,\,5\right), & r_p(t)&=\operatorname{clip}(t,10,200)^{-p}. \end{aligned} \label{eq:powerlaw} \end{equation} \emph{Inverse frequency} (IF) uses the training-signal count $n_k$ in each populated $5\GeV$ bin over $25$--$100\GeV$, with $\bar n$ their mean; outside these bins, $r_{\mathrm{IF}}=1$. Rare bins receive larger weights, approximately balancing their total influence. \emph{Power-law weighting} varies smoothly: $p=-1$ doubles the weight when energy doubles away from the clamp, whereas $p=0$ recovers BCE. Since soft taus dominate the sample, both IF and negative $p$ shift learning towards rarer, cleaner energetic examples without resampling the data. This often helped more than further emphasising ambiguous low-energy taus, but depended on the inputs. Full profiles, scans and the transfer hypothesis appear in \cref{app:weighting}; comparisons are in \cref{app:analysis_weighting}.

\paragraph{A constrained trigger objective.} A fixed weight profile applies the same emphasis whether or not a protection is at risk. Our last step therefore optimises the trigger objective itself. It had a second, more general aim: to find out what a loss that truly represents the trigger problem must look like, and which properties it must have. We collect these conclusions in \cref{sec:lessons}. The problem is \begin{equation} \max_\theta\sum_{k\in\Kset_J}w_k\big[\eff_k(\theta)-\effTOB_k\big]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\FPRev(\theta)\leq\FPRtarget,\;\;\eff_k(\theta)\geq r_k\;\;(k\in\Kset_C). \label{eq:constrained} \end{equation} In the original MLP formulation, the regions to improve, $\Kset_J=\{[25,32),[32,40),[40,60)\}\GeV$, are kept separate from the regions to protect, $\Kset_C=\Kset_J\cup\{[60,120)\}$. The saturated region is protected but not rewarded, because there is almost no room for gain there and its measurement is dominated by noise. The CNN extension also rewards $60$--$100\GeV$ and splits the saturation guards (\cref{app:constrained}). We train on the Lagrangian of~\eqref{eq:constrained}: \begin{equation} \mathcal{L}(\theta,\lambda)= -\underbrace{\sum_{k\in\Kset_J}w_k\big[\tilde\eff_k(\theta)-\effTOB_k\big]}_{\text{reward: turn-on gain}} +\lambda_{\mathrm{FPR}}\underbrace{\frac{\widetilde{\FPR}(\theta)-\FPRtarget}{\FPRtarget}}_{\text{fake-rate violation}} +\sum_{k\in\Kset_C}\lambda_k\underbrace{\big(r_k-\tilde\eff_k(\theta)\big)}_{\text{deficit in region }k}. \label{eq:lagrangian} \end{equation} \begin{itemize} \item The \emph{reward} is the efficiency gain over the baseline in the turn-on regions. For the MLP, its fixed weights $w=(0.35,0.35,0.30)$ state our physics preference. They are not learned, because an optimiser allowed to choose them would put all the weight on the easiest region. \item The \emph{fake-rate term} measures the violation relative to the $0.5\%$ target. Without this normalisation, an excess of one per mille would be numerically invisible next to an efficiency deficit of the same physical importance. \item Each \emph{region term} compares the efficiency with a floor $r_k$. The floor requires a small margin over the baseline and allows at most a small loss relative to the pretrained starting model. \item The multipliers $\lambda\geq0$ act as adaptive prices. The network parameters $\theta$ descend on $\mathcal{L}$ with Adam. Each price starts at zero, rises by projected dual ascent only while its constraint is \emph{measured} to be violated by the exact deployed rule, and falls back when it is satisfied~\cite{cotter2019proxy}. A fixed weight profile is the special case in which these prices are guessed in advance. \end{itemize} The hard threshold and two-object event rule have no useful gradient, so training uses smooth approximations while constraint checks use exact decisions. Four choices stabilise this separation: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] \item \textbf{Recalibrate the proxy threshold.} A batch-wise background quantile prevents uniformly raising all scores from appearing to improve classification. \item \textbf{Anneal the temperature.} A broad early sigmoid reaches more objects; cooling from $0.10$ to $0.02$ sharpens it towards the hard decision. \item \textbf{Measure violations out of sample.} Cross-fitting on a held-out $30\%$ of training events prevents optimistic in-sample estimates from suppressing the dual updates. \item \textbf{Start from a trained model and respect uncertainty.} Fine-tune a BCE-based checkpoint, allow statistically meaningful tolerances and calibrate deployment conservatively. \end{enumerate} \Cref{app:constrained} gives the equations, feasibility rules and discarded variants.

\subsection{Architectures} \label{sec:arch} Every model in this paper is assembled from the same parts (\cref{fig:arch}a). Optional convolutional branches read the core tensor and the EM2 image, their outputs are concatenated with scalar inputs, and a $[32,16]$ dense head produces the object score. The model names in \cref{tab:naming} describe which parts are used.

\paragraph{MLP.} The reference model is the $[32,16]$ ReLU MLP with a sigmoid output of~\cite{kernan2026}. On the 45 core cells plus $\Frac$ (\CT+\Ffeat, 46 inputs) it has $2{,}049$ parameters. Larger MLPs did not help~\cite{kernan2026}, so we looked for a better inductive bias rather than more capacity.

\paragraph{Convolutions on the core tensor.} A flat MLP must learn from data that neighbouring cells are adjacent. A convolution builds in locality and weight sharing instead. Many hand-made features are in fact fixed convolutions followed by pooling; $\Frac$, for example, is an all-ones $3\times3$ kernel, a global maximum and a division. We tested four backbones on the $5\times3\times3$ tensor. V1 mixes the five layers at every cell ($1\times1\times5$ kernel) and learns longitudinal profiles. V2 learns local spatial patterns ($2\times2\times5$ kernel). V3 applies them in series, and V4 in parallel. Because the window is centred on the TOB seed, position matters, so the maps are flattened rather than pooled. \Cref{app:vbackbones} explains each backbone step by step, and \cref{fig:cnn_blocks}a draws them.

\paragraph{A branch for the full-granularity EM2 layer.} Following~\cite{ayyar2020cnn,icecube2025cnn,kim2023hotspots}, the $12\times12$ EM2 image gets its own branch. E1 applies one $3\times3$ convolution with four filters and $2\times2$ max pooling. E2 adds a second convolution block. E3 learns its down-sampling with a stride-2 convolution. The \emph{dual-branch} model concatenates a V-backbone, an E-branch and optionally $\Frac$ into one head. \Cref{app:ebranches} and \cref{fig:cnn_blocks}b give the details.

\paragraph{Is $\Frac$ still needed next to the EM2 branch?} Although $\Frac$ is derived from EM2, a small CNN need not learn its global normalisation easily. We therefore compare matched models with and without the scalar: does an explicit scale-free ratio complement learned local patterns? The ablation is reported in \cref{app:analysis_representation}; the architectural rationale is in \cref{app:fraction_complementarity}.

\paragraph{Towards a smaller model: EM2 only.} EM2's strong contribution motivated removing the core convolution, but not the core measurements: the 45 cells or 15 layer summaries enter the dense head as scalars beside the E-branch and $\Frac$. This tests whether spatial processing is worth its parameter cost (\cref{app:em2only,app:analysis_representation}).

\paragraph{Stability and simplicity.} Every convolution is followed by BatchNorm~\cite{ioffe2015batchnorm} and LeakyReLU~\cite{maas2013leaky}, which keeps training stable on this highly imbalanced data. Inputs are standardised energies (\cref{app:arch}). Their performance is compared in \cref{sec:analysis}. All parameter counts are listed in \cref{tab:params}.

\begin{figure}[t] \centering \resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{figures/fig_architecture}} \caption{Overview of the single-object pipeline. (a) How every model is assembled: optional convolutional branches on the core tensor (V1--V4) and on the EM2 image (E1--E3), concatenated with scalar inputs such as $\Frac$, feed a $[32,16]$ head. The MLP uses flat inputs only. (b) How object scores become an event decision (\cref{sec:setting,sec:input_unit}): one shared network scores every TOB; the OR classifier also accepts an object when $q_{e,i}=\ptTOB\geq C$; the event fires with at least two accepted objects.} \label{fig:arch} \end{figure}

\subsection{Input unit: single-object and pair-object models} \label{sec:input_unit} \paragraph{Single-object models.} All models above score each TOB independently, with one shared network applied to that object's inputs. The event decision is taken afterwards by the counting rule~\eqref{eq:event_decision} or by the OR rule~\eqref{eq:or} (\cref{fig:arch}b). The decision is therefore independent of TOB order. One small circuit can be replicated for every TOB slot. Training uses object labels, while calibration and evaluation are done at event level. The price is that the network sees no event context: an event-level input is identical for all objects of an event, so it cannot rank them.
\paragraph{Pair-object models.}
sections/05_results.tex: \FloatBarrier \section{Results and Benchmarking} \label{sec:results} Our results use the fixed-rate protocol of \cref{sec:setting}: achieved event fake rates are $0.498$--$0.499\%$, band efficiencies pool tau counts, and entries are three-seed means with standard errors. Checkpoints and OR budgets are selected on validation; test-background recalibration is used only for fixed-rate reporting. Ranking finished configurations is descriptive, not a further unbiased test. The prior-work reference has a different protocol (\cref{app:prior_reference}). \Cref{tab:naming} decodes all model names; IF denotes inverse-frequency weighting, whereas $p$ denotes the separate $t^{-p}$ profile.

\subsection{Benchmark: performance under different size and plateau requirements} \label{sec:benchmark} \Cref{tab:results_main} selects the highest-global-efficiency model satisfying each row's criterion. \emph{All bands} means that the three-seed mean exceeds the baseline in every reported band, not that every seed does so. These are candidates for hardware evaluation, not validated FPGA implementations.

\begin{figure}[H] \centering \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_results_main.pdf} \caption{(a) Benchmark turn-ons; model numbers refer to \cref{tab:results_main}. The inset shows saturation, and the lower panel shows gains over the eFEX baseline. Shading indicates statistical uncertainty. (b) Prior-work NN and baseline fits from~\cite{kernan2026}, shown as a separate historical reference. The newly supplied band averages in \cref{tab:results_main} are not point samples of this fit (\cref{app:prior_reference}). Model-name key: \cref{tab:naming}.} \label{fig:results_main} \par\medskip \begingroup \centering \captionof{table}{Benchmark efficiencies [\%] by true-$\pT$ band [GeV]. Red marks our values below the baseline; counts include BatchNorm. The prior-work row is a separately evaluated reference, not part of the ranking. Model-name key: \cref{tab:naming}; provenance: \cref{app:prior_reference}.} \label{tab:results_main} \small \setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt} \input{tables/tab_main} \endgroup \end{figure}

The practical trade-off is clear: all five models turn on earlier, but the highest global efficiency, strongest plateau and smallest network do not coincide. The compact MLP retains much of the CNN gain at less than a quarter of the largest model's size. Seed-level plateau behaviour and the NN-only alternative to the compact OR model are detailed in \cref{app:benchmark_detail}.

\subsection{What the results tell us} \label{sec:analysis} \Cref{fig:results_analysis} highlights two controlled comparisons. The supporting tables, uncertainties and broader evidence are collected in \cref{app:analysis_weighting,app:analysis_representation,app:analysis_capacity,app:analysis_loss}.

\begin{figure}[t] \centering \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_results_analysis.pdf} \caption{(a) Remaining OR trade-off after inverse-frequency (IF) weighting: adding the comparator exchanges low-energy efficiency for plateau gains. Both sides use IF; the BCE-to-IF comparison is in \cref{tab:analysis}. (b) Effect of adding EM2 and $\Frac$, then removing the core convolution. Abbreviations: \cref{tab:naming}. Supporting comparisons: \cref{app:analysis_weighting,app:analysis_representation}.} \label{fig:results_analysis} \end{figure}

\paragraph{(a) More weight on energetic taus can help.} The results support the hypothesis in \cref{sec:loss}: emphasising energetic rather than soft taus often helped. Compared with BCE, IF reduced the selected TOB budget (\cref{tab:analysis}). \Cref{fig:results_analysis}a shows the resulting trade-off: after IF training, OR buys a small plateau gain at a larger low-energy cost, so NN-only can win globally. This is input-dependent, not a universal preference for IF or negative $p$ (\cref{app:analysis_weighting}).

\paragraph{(b) Spatial learning and engineered features complement each other.} CNNs recovered some taus missed by the MLP, consistent with sensitivity to spatial shower patterns. The larger gain came from the fine-grained EM2 input; adding $\Frac$ remained useful, while removing the core convolution retained most performance with fewer parameters (\cref{app:analysis_representation}).

\paragraph{(c) More parameters were not the main route to improvement.} Wider MLPs and deeper CNNs gave no systematic advantage in the tested families. Similar errors across core-only models point to limited input discrimination rather than insufficient capacity (\cref{app:analysis_capacity}).

\paragraph{(d) The objective controls the trade-off across energies.} Constrained fine-tuning redistributed efficiency towards protected or rewarded regions, usually with a small global change. The best loss depended on the inputs, and the lowest-energy band remained difficult across methods (\cref{app:analysis_loss}).
sections/06_lessons.tex: \paragraph{Design the loss for the decision.} Building a task-specific loss meant translating the trigger into rewards, protected regions and a fake-rate constraint, rather than merely choosing a standard classification loss. Its value was control over the efficiency profile, not a guaranteed global gain (\cref{sec:loss,app:analysis_loss}).

\paragraph{More gradient is not more learnability.} We initially up-weighted difficult low-energy taus to improve their efficiency; this often hurt. Emphasising cleaner, higher-energy examples worked better for several inputs. Our working explanation is that useful class structure can transfer, whereas ambiguous examples may consume gradient without improving separation. Weighting must reflect what the data and model can learn, not only where we want improvement; this is a problem-dependent lesson (\cref{app:weighting,app:analysis_weighting}).

\paragraph{Understand the input before enlarging the model.} The earlier MLP sweep tested networks up to roughly $100$ times larger without improving its small reference, while our gains came from fine-grained EM2 information and compactness features. We learned to question input discrimination before blaming capacity: a larger network cannot restore detail absent from its inputs (\cref{sec:features,app:analysis_capacity,app:analysis_representation}).

\paragraph{Complexity must earn its parameters.} Deeper or strided EM2 branches did not systematically beat the simple E1. Local patterns and their positions may already suffice on these small images; E1's dense head also combines them globally, while further compression can lose detail. This is a plausible explanation, not proof of why a particular model lost. We therefore favour the smallest architecture that preserves the required efficiency profile (\cref{sec:arch,app:analysis_capacity}).

\paragraph{Loss (function), but not for nothing.} We learned three design requirements the hard way: (i)~reward better ranking, not score inflation; (ii)~give every relevant energy region an explicit reward or protection, or it can be sacrificed; and (iii)~ensure gradients reach missed signal, not just objects already near the threshold. Exact out-of-sample checks and statistically meaningful tolerances complete the recipe. \Cref{app:loss_requirements} details all five lessons and the failures that revealed them.
sections/07_future.tex: \section{Tau be continued} \label{sec:future} Four directions follow from the remaining accuracy--resource trade-off: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Smaller CNNs.} Reduce channels and head widths, prune, quantise and distil strong models into compact students; validate the resulting efficiency, latency and FPGA resource use. \item \textbf{Adaptive loss design.} Derive target regions and tolerances from the starting model's weaknesses, with uncertainty-aware updates that adapt to the input representation. \item \textbf{Whole-event learning.} Vary the number of input objects and design an event-level architecture that can learn dependencies between candidates, rather than scoring each in isolation. \item \textbf{Richer detector inputs.} The limited detector information available to our models leaves low-energy tau and background deposits difficult to distinguish. Richer measurements and finer spatial resolution at the input stage could therefore be crucial, rather than further model complexity alone. \end{itemize} \Cref{app:future} develops these directions and their evaluation requirements.
